name: Mooren ulcer
aliases: chronic serpiginous ulcer of the cornea

reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A painful, progressive, idiopathic peripheral ulcerative keratitis that spreads circumferentially and centrally from the limbus
The ulcer has a characteristic overhanging, undermined leading edge with an intact epithelium beyond the advancing margin
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, made only after autoimmune and infective causes of peripheral ulcerative keratitis have been ruled out
A limited unilateral form typically affects older patients, while an aggressive bilateral form is more common in younger patients and can be relentless
Severe pain, out of proportion to signs, together with progressive thinning is typical
There is no scleral involvement, which helps distinguish it from Terrien degeneration and from scleritis-associated peripheral keratitis
Management follows an immunosuppressive ladder from topical corticosteroids to systemic immunomodulators, with conjunctival resection and surgical repair for perforation
An association with hepatitis C has been described in some aggressive cases and is worth considering
reference.pathophysiology: Mooren ulcer is thought to be an autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis in which an immune response against corneal stromal antigens leads to progressive destruction. Autoantibodies and cell-mediated inflammation recruit neutrophils and activate collagenolytic and proteolytic enzymes from the limbal vessels and adjacent conjunctiva, degrading peripheral corneal stroma. The ulcer advances circumferentially and centrally with a characteristic undermined edge, and the sclera is spared. Progressive stromal melting can lead to marked thinning, irregular astigmatism, and perforation. Because the process is inflammatory rather than infective, treatment is directed at suppressing the immune response.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis from systemic vasculitis (e.g. granulomatosis with polyangiitis, rheumatoid arthritis)
Infective peripheral keratitis (bacterial, herpetic, fungal, acanthamoeba)
Dellen and other non-inflammatory peripheral thinning
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting the undermined advancing edge and degree of thinning
Corneal scrapings and cultures to exclude infective keratitis
Systemic autoimmune and vasculitis workup (including inflammatory markers and autoantibodies) to exclude secondary peripheral ulcerative keratitis
Hepatitis C serology in aggressive or bilateral disease
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography or pachymetry to monitor thinning
Corneal topography to assess induced astigmatism
redFlags: Rapidly progressive thinning threatening or causing perforation
Severe unremitting pain with an advancing undermined edge
Bilateral aggressive disease in a younger patient
Features suggesting an underlying systemic vasculitis requiring urgent systemic treatment
reference.prognosis: The limited unilateral form in older patients often responds to treatment, whereas the bilateral aggressive form can be relentless, causing severe thinning, perforation, and significant visual loss despite immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Mooren ulcer without first excluding systemic vasculitis and infection
Missing scleral involvement that would point away from Mooren ulcer
Undertreating aggressive disease and allowing progression to perforation
Overlooking an associated systemic condition such as hepatitis C
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Suppress the autoimmune process, beginning with intensive topical corticosteroids and escalating to systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as ciclosporin, methotrexate or cyclophosphamide for aggressive or bilateral disease
Limit stromal melting with collagenase inhibitors and generous lubrication, and avoid topical anaesthetic misuse
Control the severe pain and support the ocular surface
Surgical and adjunctive measures for progressive thinning or perforation, including conjunctival resection or recession, tissue adhesive, amniotic membrane grafting or tectonic corneal grafting
Investigate and treat associated systemic disease, including hepatitis C, where antiviral therapy can improve virus-associated cases
Regular monitoring of thinning with anterior segment optical coherence tomography or pachymetry and vigilance for perforation, under corneal specialist care
